title: Romans 12:1–8
context: The long argument of chapters 1–11 turns into worship. Paul appeals by the mercies of God already displayed: present your bodies a living sacrifice, refuse the world’s mold, and take your place in one body whose gifts differ by grace.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about the living sacrifice and the one body whose gifts differ by grace.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: I exhort you—St. Paul uses to suit his exhortations to the doctrines he has been delivering. So here the general use from the whole is contained in the first and second verses. By the tender mercies of God—the entire gospel, the whole economy of grace or mercy, delivering us from the wrath of God, and exciting us to all duty. To present—now actually to exhibit before God. Your bodies—that is, yourselves. A sacrifice—dead to sin and living. A Christian acts in all things by the highest reason, from the mercy of God inferring his own duty.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Rom 12:1)

reformed.quote: Paul lays down here the principle from which all the duties of holiness flow, even this—that we are redeemed by the Lord for this end—that we may consecrate to him ourselves and all our members. It is then the beginning of a right course in good works, when we understand that we are consecrated to the Lord; for it hence follows that we must cease to live to ourselves, in order that we may devote all the actions of our life to his service. By calling it living, he intimates that we are sacrificed to the Lord for this end—that our former life being destroyed in us, we may be raised up to a new life.

verses.text: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore” rests on mercy already preached, yet the appeal is no formality: present your bodies. Wesley heard the whole economy of grace delivering from wrath and exciting to duty—mercy inferred as one’s own offering. The sacrifice is living, holy, acceptable: the whole self actually exhibited before God, not a dead animal and not a private idea of devotion.

Arminian interpreters read this as enabled consecration that must still be presented. Prevenient and cooperating grace make the offering possible; the worshiper is not a spectator of a work God performs without him. Spiritual worship is the reasonable answer of those who, having received mercy, yield themselves. Holiness is response—and the response is sincerely required.
verses.reformedNotes:
Mercies (chs. 1–11) are not a footnote; they are the engine. Calvin: we are redeemed for this end—that we may consecrate ourselves. The living sacrifice is what mercy produces in a people God has made His own. Former life destroyed, new life raised: the offering is God’s work in those He has claimed. We are not our own; we have passed over to become His property.

Holiness is response, not a ladder into mercy. God works the presentation He commands. The church’s worship comes from election, calling, and justification already set forth. “Therefore” is ethics from prior grace, not a new bargain.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat the living sacrifice as holy response to mercy. Arminians underline enabled consecration that must actually be presented—grace that can be yielded to or neglected. Reformed readers press that the mercies of chapters 1–11 produce the offering God Himself works in His people.

verses.text: Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.
verses.arminianNotes:
Two voices: do not be conformed; be transformed. Wesley: neither in judgment, spirit, nor behaviour; this world neglects God’s will and follows its own. Renewal of mind is grace at work in the believer who must still refuse the age’s mold. Discernment of the good, acceptable, and perfect will is the fruit of a self already presented—known by sure trial.

Transformation is authentic and responsible. The mind can be renewed; the will of God can be proved by those who cooperate with the Spirit rather than sliding back into the world’s pattern. The command is sincere: conformity is not fate, and renewal is not a spectator sport.
verses.reformedNotes:
Conformity to this world is the old man; transformation is newness of mind. Calvin: renovation is not of the flesh only but of the mind, the leading power—Paul pulls reason down from her throne. We prove God’s will by bidding adieu to our own counsels. The world invents “good”; God defines it in His commandments. Nothing pleases Him except what He has commanded.

The mind is renewed because God regenerates. Discernment is gift before it is skill—the Spirit’s effectual work in those already made alive. The will of God is good, acceptable, and perfect because it is His, not because we have improved it.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse worldly conformity and seek a renewed mind. Arminians typically describe transformation as grace-enabled yet resistible renewal the believer must pursue; Reformed commentators often describe it as the Spirit’s effectual renovation of minds God has already claimed.

verses.text: For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.
verses.arminianNotes:
Grace given to Paul grounds a word to everyone: do not think more highly than you ought. Sober judgment matches the measure of faith God has assigned. Wesley: the measure of faith treated of in the opening chapters, from which all other gifts and graces flow. Pride is the first enemy of the body’s peace.

The measure is God’s gift among those who believe. Assignment does not void responsible humility; it summons it. Each is to think and serve within what grace has actually given. High thoughts of self are a refusal of the grace that made room for every member.
verses.reformedNotes:
Paul speaks through the grace of apostleship, not self-made stature. God has distributed the measure of faith; sober thinking stays inside that allotment. Calvin: it is part of our reasonable sacrifice to surrender ourselves, meek and teachable, to be ruled by God; the faithful humbly keep themselves within the limits allotted to them.

Assignment is the Lord’s. High thoughts of self trespass on God’s measuring. Humility is sanity about a grace we did not invent. The body will be safe when no one exceeds the portion God was pleased to give.
verses.keyContrast: Both credit God with measuring faith and gifts. Arminians hear a gracious assignment to believers who must still walk humbly in what they have received; Reformed commentators typically hear God’s sovereign distribution that both limits and enables each member.

verses.text: For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
verses.arminianNotes:
One body, many members, different functions. Variety is not a problem to solve; it is how a body works. No member is the whole, and no function is surplus.

Differing functions are gifts to be used, not ranks to defend. Grace that joined us to Christ also joins us to one another’s need. The body’s health depends on members actually serving in the function given, not coveting another’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
The body simile confirms vocation. Calvin: Christ has ordained a fellowship like the members of the human body, and He Himself is the bond of the connection. Functions differ because God distributed them.

No member possesses all powers, nor may it seize another’s office. God has determined the order He would have observed among us. Comparison is a misreading of the Giver.

verses.text: so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,
verses.arminianNotes:
Many, yet one body in Christ, members one of another. Wesley: all believers, closely connected together in Christ, and consequently ought to be helpful to each other. Belonging is mutual: we do not float as private Christians.

Oneness in Christ is true for all who are in Him by faith. Membership one of another is a duty of help, not a metaphor to admire. The connection can be honored or neglected; grace enables the help it requires.
verses.reformedNotes:
Union with Christ is the body’s life; membership one of another is its shape. God has made a people, not a pile of individuals. The many are one because they are in Christ.

Helpfulness is the ethic of a union God established. We do not manufacture the body; we occupy the place we have been given in it, for the common good of what He has joined.

verses.text: having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
verses.arminianNotes:
Gifts differ according to the grace that was given; use them. Wesley: gifts are various, grace is one. Prophecy here is chiefly the ordinary gift of expounding Scripture, according to the analogy of faith—the grand scheme of original sin, justification by faith, and present inward salvation.

Grace given is to be exercised. The Giver enables; the member must prophesy, serve, and speak in proportion to faith received, not bury the gift. Differing gifts are not a ranking of worth but a call to spend what has been placed in our hands.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: no one is furnished with fullness of gifts, lest he despise his brethren. Difference of gifts proceeds not from the will of man but because it has pleased the Lord to distribute His grace in this manner. Prophecy is tested by the analogy of faith, the first principles of religion.

Use is obedience inside a sovereign distribution. The church is safe when each imparts what he received without trespassing on another’s function. To invert the order is to fight with God.

verses.text: or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
verses.arminianNotes:
Service in serving; the teacher in teaching. Offices are for the work named, not for display. Wesley: ministering as deacons; teachers of catechumens, for whom particular instructors were appointed.

Grace makes the task possible and required. Stay in the work given; do it fully. The body is helped when gifts are actually spent on the people they were given for, not held as titles.
verses.reformedNotes:
Let the minister fulfill the office by ministering faithfully, that he may answer to his name. Calvin: the teacher studies this one thing—that the church may be instructed; he who excels in teaching knows the end is that the church may be built by the word of truth.

Function is stewardship. God assigned the post; faithfulness in it is the calling, not a search for a more impressive gift. The name of the office is a summons to the work.

verses.text: or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
verses.arminianNotes:
Exhortation, generosity, leading with zeal, mercy with cheerfulness. The list ends in tone: open-handed, eager, glad. Wesley: the one who presides has the care of a flock; the one who shows mercy, in any instance, rejoices that he has such an opportunity.

These are graces to be practiced. Cheerful mercy is commanded because grace can form it. Leading with zeal is love of the flock, not love of rank. The exhortation is sincere—the Spirit enables a gladness in the work of help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: givers in simplicity, without fraud or respect of persons; those who show mercy without peevishness, lest they mar the favor conferred; presidents watching day and night for the flock’s wellbeing. Cheerfulness is part of the gift’s proper use: the distressed are consoled by prompt, glad help and wounded by a grim face.

God distributes not only the office but the manner. Zeal and cheerfulness are the Spirit’s way of keeping the body’s care from becoming grim duty. The Lord who assigned the gift assigns its tone.
